sections.title: The first ten minutes
sections.intro: The call starts. These three questions come up in nearly every behavioral round, usually in this order. Play it through.

questions.prompt: "So, tell me about yourself." What's the right structure?
options: Every job in order, oldest to newest, ~5 min
How you got into tech as a kid, then today
"It's all on my resume" — then ask a question
Summary → 2-3 accomplishments → why this role, ~60s
questions.explanation: Personal summary, accomplishments, then a forward-looking statement, in 30-90 seconds. The others are the classic mistakes: the History Lesson, the Childhood Origin Story, and Less Is Not More.

questions.prompt: Which accomplishment belongs in your TMAY?
options: Your academic GPA and graduation honors
The full CARL story of your best project
One line that previews your flagship project
A list of every tool and language you know
questions.explanation: Keep each to a sentence, focused on business impact. Ideally one overlaps with your favorite-project answer, which steers the next question toward your strongest material.

questions.prompt: You left your last job partly out of frustration with leadership. In your forward-looking statement, you say:
options: Nothing — skip the forward-looking part
That you needed to get out quickly
What you want next, and why this role fits it
That your last company was badly run
questions.explanation: Talk about what you're moving toward, not what you're leaving. Criticizing a former employer reads as a judgment flag, however justified the frustration was.

questions.prompt: Next: "What's the most impactful thing you've worked on?" Which story do you tell?
options: The biggest project your company ever ran
Whichever story you told most recently
A different story than your favorite project
Your flagship story — the same one "favorite" would get
questions.explanation: "Favorite," "most impactful," and "ambiguous problem you solved" are the same question underneath. Have one flagship story, picked for Impact → Scope → Personal Contribution.

questions.prompt: Your choices: a huge company-wide launch where you owned one small piece, or a smaller project you fully led. Which is the flagship?
options: Neither — pick whichever is most recent
The smaller one you led — Personal Contribution wins
The big launch — Scope always wins
Both — tell them back to back
questions.explanation: If no project scores high on all three, put Personal Contribution first. They need to see your decisions, and a peripheral role in a big project has none to show.

questions.prompt: Then: "Tell me about a time you had a conflict." Which story do you choose?
options: High stakes, you were central, your position was defensible
Low stakes, so it can't be held against you
One where you were clearly wrong, to show humility
One you watched happen between two other people
questions.explanation: The stakes are a scope signal, central involvement shows your actions, and a defensible position is lower risk. If they explicitly ask for a time you were *wrong*, pick one where your initial view was reasonable given what you knew at the time.

questions.prompt: Your story ends: "…and we went with the hybrid approach." What's missing?
options: Who was ultimately right in the end
How the relationship stood afterward
The exact technical spec of the hybrid
Nothing — the decision is the result
questions.explanation: The Result has to include the relationship, ideally with proof you worked well together later. Companies are trying hard not to hire someone who's difficult to work with.

questions.prompt: Finally: "Any questions for me?" Which is the strongest?
options: "What's the salary range and PTO policy?"
"So — how do you think I did?"
"No, I think you covered everything."
"What's the hardest problem this team faces this year?"
questions.explanation: Prepare 3-5 questions for each interviewer, matched to who they are. Save compensation for the recruiter. "How did I do?" puts them in an awkward spot, and "no questions" wastes the last chance to show interest.

questions.snippet: "It's honestly been my life's dream to work at a company like yours."
options: Too short — expand on why it's a dream
Flattery — it spends the most attentive seconds on nothing
Strong — enthusiasm is what they're looking for
Fine, as long as it's sincere
questions.explanation: The first 20 seconds set the tone, and they're when the interviewer is paying closest attention. Spend them on the summary that steers toward your best material.

questions.prompt: A candidate had a 6-month gap. Best way to handle it in TMAY?
options: Briefly address skill atrophy: what you learned meanwhile
Explain the personal reasons in full detail
Apologize for it at the start
Leave it out and hope nobody asks
questions.explanation: Tell the story yourself, briefly, and answer the concern behind it. For a gap, that's skill atrophy; for a layoff, performance risk; for short stints, commitment.

questions.prompt: A conflict story told like this:
questions.snippet: "The PM and I had a small difference of opinion, and we quickly found common ground."
options: Over-sanitized — no believable friction or emotion
Ideal — calm and professional throughout
Too long — conflict stories should be brief
Fine, if they add a metric at the end
questions.explanation: If someone was genuinely upset, say so, in an even, factual tone. That's what proves you can handle charged situations. Sanding the friction off removes the evidence.

questions.prompt: In a conflict, the candidate escalated straight to their manager without talking to the other engineer first. How does this read?
options: Well — managers should resolve conflicts
Neutral — the channel doesn't matter
Poorly — go to the source before escalating
Well — it shows respect for hierarchy
questions.explanation: Tech companies look for people who go directly to the source and are willing to be assertive. Bring in more people at the right time, not first.

questions.prompt: Where can a real conflict story come from, if there was no interpersonal drama?
options: Tech choices, priorities, timelines, resources, process
Nowhere — say you don't have conflicts
Only fights with a manager count
Only disputes that went to HR count
questions.explanation: Database choices, features vs. tech debt, shipping vs. safety, resource allocation, introducing new tooling against resistance. These are all legitimate, and often better, conflict stories.

questions.snippet: "I'm open to really anything, whatever the team needs."
options: Fine — the forward-looking part doesn't matter
Too specific — keep it even more open
Ideal — flexibility is always valued
Too deferential — senior candidates should name what they want
questions.explanation: The more senior you are, the more confident this statement should be about what you're looking for. Vague openness reads as not knowing your own direction.
